text: The applicants' details are set out in the appended table.
The Government were represented by Mr G. Matyushkin, Representative of the Russian Federation at the European Court of Human Rights.
The Government were subsequently represented by Mr A. Fedorov, Head of the Office of the Representative of the Russian Federation at the European Court of Human Rights.
The Government were subsequently represented by Mr M. Galperin, Representative of the Russian Federation at the European Court of Human Rights.
The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows.
On 24 February 2014, the final hearing in the criminal case concerning the mass disorder at Bolotnaya Square in Moscow on 6 May 2012 took place at the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow.
Seven participants in the events at Bolotnaya Square in Moscow on 6 May 2012 were sentenced to prison terms of two and a half years and four years.
The criminal proceedings concerning the mass disorder at Bolotnaya Square in Moscow on 6 May 2012 were considered by many to be driven by political reasons.
The criminal proceedings concerning the mass disorder at Bolotnaya Square in Moscow on 6 May 2012 attracted a lot of public and media attention.
In the evening of 24 February 2014, a public gathering in support of the convicted activists took place at Tverskaya Street in Moscow.
In the evening of 24 February 2014, a public gathering in support of the convicted activists took place at Malaya Sadovaya Street in St Petersburg.
The public meetings on 24 February 2014 at Tverskaya Street in Moscow and at Malaya Sadovaya Street in St Petersburg had been advertised on social media.
The authorities had not been notified of the public gatherings on 24 February 2014 at Tverskaya Street in Moscow and at Malaya Sadovaya Street in St Petersburg.
The applicants took part in the public meetings on 24 February 2014 at Tverskaya Street in Moscow and at Malaya Sadovaya Street in St Petersburg.
There is no information that the public meetings on 24 February 2014 at Tverskaya Street in Moscow and at Malaya Sadovaya Street in St Petersburg turned violent.
The protesters at the public meetings on 24 February 2014 shouted political slogans.
The police warned the protesters at the public meetings on 24 February 2014 through megaphones that the gatherings had not been authorised.
The police instructed the protesters at the public meetings on 24 February 2014 to disperse.
The applicants were apprehended and transferred to various police stations following the public meetings on 24 February 2014.

On the dates stipulated in the appended table, the applicants were convicted under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences for breaching the procedure for the organisation or conduct of public gatherings.
The applicants were sentenced to fines ranging between 10,000 Russian roubles (RUB 10,000) and RUB 20,000, as set out in the appended table.
The applicant in application no. 3093/15 was convicted under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences for a refusal to obey a lawful order of a police officer.
The applicant in application no. 3093/15 was ordered to pay RUB 1,000.
The domestic courts in the case of the applicant in application no. 3093/15 relied on the administrative record, the reports and explanations of the police officers.

The domestic courts considered it unlawful that the applicant in application no. 3093/15 shouted slogans during a public assembly in respect of which no advance notification had been submitted to the authorities.

The domestic courts considered it unlawful that the applicant in application no. 3093/15 refused to stop participating in a public assembly in respect of which no advance notification had been submitted to the authorities.
For a summary of the relevant domestic law, see Navalnyy v. Russia [GC] (nos. 29580/12 and 4 others, §§ 46-47, 15 November 2018).
The domestic legal provisions governing administrative transfer (escorting) and detention are set out in the case of Butkevich v. Russia (no. 5865/07, §§ 33-36, 13 February 2018).

According to Article 31.9 of the Code of Administrative Offences, if a decision imposing an administrative punishment is not enforced during two years from its entry into force, it can no longer be executed.

According to Article 31.9 of the Code of Administrative Offences, the time when the enforcement of a decision imposing an administrative punishment is suspended or stayed is excluded from the two-year period after which the decision can no longer be executed.
